narrative:
The model predicted a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaled to the model that your later-year performance was weaker than most successful applicants. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; a third-decile placement is well below the sixth-decile average of those who were admitted.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore gave the model some reason to expect you might pass. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the two class-rank indicators.

Your LSAT score of 35 was slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, your high family income is relatively uncommon among admitted students, and your plans to attend full-time are typical. Gender and race played no role in the model's decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Raising your class standing in future years or boosting your LSAT score would most directly address the factors that worked against you. Consider reapplying once you have demonstrated clearer evidence of consistent high performance.
